lead: The word of God “continued to advance”, and in Antioch the Holy Spirit speaks while the Church is at worship: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul”. Mission is born of liturgy and fasting. In the Gospel Jesus gives his last public summary: he has come as light, not to judge the world but to save it. Psalm 67 prays that God’s saving power be known among all nations. Today is the optional memorial of St Anselm, who wrote that he believed in order to understand.

set: Chapter 12 ends with the death of Herod Agrippa I and the growth of the word of God (12:23–24): persecutors pass, and the word remains. Barnabas and Saul had taken famine relief from Antioch to Jerusalem (11:29–30) and now return with John Mark. From here on Antioch, not Jerusalem, is the base of the mission to the nations, and Saul moves to the center of the story.
str: 12:24–25: the word grows; Barnabas and Saul return with John Mark.
13:2–3: the Spirit speaks at worship; fasting, prayer, laying on of hands.
13:4–5a: sent by the Spirit to Seleucia, Cyprus and Salamis.
kw: to worship, to serve in the liturgy
The word behind our “liturgy” (13:2). The Spirit speaks while the community is at worship and fasting. The great missionary journeys begin not from a planning meeting but from prayer.
Paul will use the same verb of himself: “set apart for the gospel of God” (Romans 1:1). To be set apart is not to be cut off from people but to be dedicated to a task for them.
member of the court, one brought up with

Manaen had been brought up with Herod Antipas, the tetrarch who beheaded John the Baptist. The list of leaders joins a Levite from Cyprus, Simeon called Niger (“black”), Lucius from Cyrene in Africa, a man of the royal court and a former persecutor. The Gospel had reached the palace and the street.
vv: Then after completing their mission Barnabas and Saul returned to Jerusalem

A known puzzle. The oldest manuscripts read “to Jerusalem”, but the story needs a return from Jerusalem to Antioch, and other manuscripts read “from Jerusalem”, as the Malayalam POC does. Some scholars read the Greek as “they returned, having completed their service in Jerusalem”.
While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said,
Luke does not say how the Spirit spoke; most likely through one of the prophets named in v. 1.
So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit,

The community laid hands on them and sent them (v. 3); Luke now says the Spirit sent them. This was not the first making of Saul an apostle, for his call came from the risen Lord (Galatians 1:1), but the Church’s blessing and sending for a particular work. The Spirit calls and the Church sends, and both are one act.
ch: The Church has always seen in this scene the pattern of mission: the initiative of the Spirit, the discernment of a community at prayer, and the sending by the Church with the laying on of hands. Pope St Paul VI wrote that evangelizing is the grace and vocation proper to the Church, her deepest identity (Evangelii Nuntiandi 14). A parish that prays and fasts together will sooner or later hear the same voice: set someone apart for the work.

r.h: I have come as light into the world
set: These verses close the first half of John’s Gospel, which many call the Book of Signs. The evangelist has just said that many did not believe, while some leaders believed in secret (12:37–43). Then, with no place or time given, Jesus “cried aloud” a last public summary of all he has said: to believe in him is to believe in the Father; he is light; he came to save; his word will judge. From chapter 13 on he speaks only to his own.
str: vv. 44–45: to believe in Jesus and to see him is to believe in and see the one who sent him.
vv. 47–48: not to judge but to save; the word as judge.
vv. 49–50: the Father’s commandment is eternal life.
kw: Used of Jesus teaching in the Temple at the feast of Tabernacles (7:28, 37). A public, urgent cry, like a prophet’s; this is the last time Jesus addresses the crowds in John.
Not only the absence of light but the world closed against God (1:5). No one who believes need “remain” there: the verb suggests that all begin in the dark, and Christ comes to lead them out.
Jesus does not come as a judge looking for the guilty. Yet a word refused becomes a judgment: the light itself shows what a person has chosen (3:19).
vv: Whoever believes in me believes not in me but in him who sent me.
Jesus never draws people to himself apart from the Father. Faith in him is the way into the Father’s own life.
I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in the darkness.
The Easter candle, carried into the dark church at the Vigil with the chant “The Light of Christ”, proclaims this verse without words.
I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.
Compare 3:17. The Father’s purpose in sending the Son is mercy.
ch: The Church reads these verses as Jesus’ own summary of the Gospel. The Catechism teaches that Christ has full right to judge, yet he came to save, and that by rejecting grace in this life a person already judges himself (CCC 679). So the Church preaches with urgency and gentleness together: the light is offered to all, and no one is forced into it.

rite: St Anselm (1033–1109), born at Aosta, was a monk and abbot of Bec in Normandy and then Archbishop of Canterbury; he is a Doctor of the Church. In his Proslogion he prays: “I do not seek to understand in order to believe, but I believe in order to understand.” His watchword, faith seeking understanding, suits today’s Gospel: whoever believes does not remain in darkness, and faith becomes a light for the mind as well as the heart.
study: What does it mean for my parish that mission is born from worship and fasting, as in Antioch?
Where in my life am I still choosing to “remain in the darkness”? What would it take to step into the light?
